transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess I'm here because I'm on leave from work right now. I work in HR, and I recently pushed ahead with our new onboarding launch. I just went ahead and committed company money and secured all the vendor time before any of the official approvals were actually in place. 

Which, you know, the vendor is based out of Chicago, and honestly, dealing with them is always an experience. Have you ever been to Chicago in the winter? The wind there is just unbelievable. I went there for an HR conference right after I finished my master's degree, and I had to buy this ridiculously expensive wool coat just to walk two blocks from the convention center to my hotel. It's still sitting in the back of my closet collecting dust. My wife keeps telling me to donate it, but I spent like four hundred dollars on it, so I just can't bring myself to get rid of it, you know how that is. 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right. At the time, pushing the launch forward just felt really bold. It felt completely necessary to just cut through all the corporate red tape and get things moving. But now... yeah, now they've put me on leave and everyone at the office is asking what I was thinking.
Did you think through the potential consequences of launching the onboarding program without official approvals before you did it?

Did I think it through? No, not really. Like I was just saying, at the exact moment I did it, it just felt... bold. Completely necessary. I felt like I was finally just getting things done, committing the funds and the vendor time without waiting for all those slow-moving gears to turn. I definitely wasn't thinking about ending up on administrative leave with the whole department asking what I was thinking. 

Speaking of thinking things through, my wife actually asked me the same thing about the landscaping we did last summer. We hired this guy to put in a retaining wall, and he brought in this massive backhoe that completely tore up the neighbor's side of the grass. The neighbor was furious, understandably. He's this retired dentist, really particular about his lawn. He uses that special fertilizer—milorganite, I think it's called? It smells terrible for a few days but his grass is incredibly green. I actually tried to buy some at Home Depot but they were totally sold out. The guy in the garden center said there's some kind of supply chain issue with it. Which is crazy, right? Everything has a supply chain issue these days. I mean, even trying to buy a car right now is a nightmare. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right. Yeah, I didn't think about the consequences at work at all. I just pushed the button.
Do you often act on impulse like you did with the onboarding program launch?

Well, I guess... I mean, I don't really know if I do it a lot. I just sort of do things when they need to be done. Like when I bought that espresso machine last month. I was just walking through Williams Sonoma—which, by the way, smells incredible in there, they always have some kind of citrus thing going on. My wife loves citrus, especially bergamot. We actually went to this tea shop downtown once that had all these different Earl Grey blends, and the owner was telling us how bergamot is actually a type of orange that grows in Italy. Italy is supposed to be beautiful in the spring, we've always talked about going to Florence or maybe Rome. I heard the pasta there is just completely different from what we have here. You know, they use a different type of flour, double zero or something like that? It makes the dough really silky. I tried making homemade pasta once during the pandemic, like everyone else did, but it just ended up being this sticky mess all over the kitchen counter. It took me hours to scrape it off. 

But um... wait, what did you ask me? Something about impulse? I don't know, I just... I haven't really kept track of if I do things like that often. I just do what feels right in the moment.
Have you acted on impulse like this throughout your life or is this a relatively recent development?

Well, I guess... no, it hasn't been my whole life. It's really just been building for about a month now. It all started when that new executive came in and started challenging my onboarding redesign. He's this guy from corporate, always wearing these incredibly flashy ties. Like, really bright patterns. It reminds me of this tie my dad used to wear to church when I was a kid. It had these little mallard ducks all over it. My dad loved duck hunting, he'd go up to this cabin in Wisconsin every November with his buddies. They'd bring back so much meat, my mom had to buy a separate chest freezer just to store it all in the garage. Which, actually, that freezer finally broke down last year and leaked water all over my golf clubs. I had to get them completely regripped, and let me tell you, golf grips have gotten ridiculously expensive. The pro shop guy told me it's because of the rubber shortage. 

But yeah... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. The executive. Yeah, he started pushing back on my ideas about a month ago, and that's when things just started... escalating, I guess. So no, it's not a lifelong thing.
Have you been feeling unusually anxious, stressed, or upset around the time you started acting on these impulses?

Well, anxious isn't really the right word. It's more like... for the past few weeks, I've felt just brilliantly alive, you know? Like I could finally show the leadership team what HR can actually be, what we can really do when we're not bogged down in red tape. Red tape is such a funny phrase, isn't it? I read once that it comes from the actual red tape they used to bind legal documents in England centuries ago. Or maybe it was Spain? I love history like that. My son is taking AP European History right now and he's doing this massive project on the French Revolution. He's been building this scale model of the Bastille out of popsicle sticks and hot glue. We had to go to three different craft stores just to find enough of the wide popsicle sticks. The cashier at Michaels was this older lady who told me she uses them to label her herb garden. She grows all her own basil and makes pesto from scratch. I love a good pesto, especially on a grilled chicken sandwich with some provolone. There's this deli near my office that makes the most incredible chicken pesto panini, they press it so the bread gets perfectly crispy on the outside. 

But um... what were we talking about? Oh, right, how I was feeling. Yeah, so I felt brilliant, but then... if someone questioned me, even over something tiny like a small edit to a document or a routine budget question, I'd get suddenly furious. Just incredibly irritable. So it was like bouncing between feeling unstoppable and just being so angry at anyone slowing me down.
Have you been feeling like you're capable of achieving things that others couldn't during this time?

Well, I guess... I mean, I haven't really thought about it like that. I just know what needs to be done, you know? Like, I can see the big picture when other people are just staring at the details. Details are important, sure, but you can't get lost in them. Like when you're painting a room. You have to step back and look at the whole wall, not just the little spot you're rolling over. My wife and I painted our living room last spring. We chose this color called "Sea Salt," it's kind of a gray-green. It changes color depending on the light, which is really cool. In the morning, it looks more green, but by the evening, it's definitely gray. We had to buy all new throw pillows to match it, because our old ones were this bright red that just completely clashed. We found some really nice linen ones at Pottery Barn. They were on sale, too, which was a nice surprise. I love a good sale. It's like a little victory, you know? Finding something you want for less than you expected to pay. My grandfather was always looking for a bargain. He used to clip coupons from the Sunday paper every week. He had this whole system, with little envelopes for different categories like groceries and hardware. He was a carpenter, actually, built half the houses in his neighborhood back in the fifties. 

But um... wait, what did you ask me? Something about achieving things? I don't know, I just... I haven't really thought about whether I'm doing things others can't. I'm just doing what I know I can do.
Do you feel like you have special talents or abilities that set you apart from others?

Well, special talents? I mean, I don't know if I'd call them special talents, exactly. I'm just really good at my job, you know? Like, I understand people. People are so fascinating. I was just reading this article about how human psychology hasn't really changed since we were hunter-gatherers. Like, our brains are still wired to look out for predators and gather berries and stuff. Speaking of berries, I tried making a mixed berry cobbler last weekend. My neighbor gave me this huge bucket of blackberries from her garden. She's got this amazing setup, raised beds and a drip irrigation system and everything. She's retired, used to be a high school chemistry teacher, so she treats her garden like a science experiment. She was telling me all about soil pH and nitrogen levels. It's actually really complicated, getting the right balance for different plants. Tomatoes, for instance, they need a lot of calcium or they get this thing called blossom end rot. I tried growing tomatoes once on my balcony when I lived in Chicago, but the pigeons kept eating them before they were ripe. Pigeons are so bold in the city, they'll just walk right up to you. I saw one steal a french fry right out of a guy's hand at Navy Pier once. 

But um... what were we talking about? Oh, right, special talents. Yeah, I don't know. I wouldn't say I have any, like, superpowers or anything. I just do my job.
Do you often feel like you're more important or special than others?

More important? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, everyone has a role to play, right? Like in an orchestra. You can't just have first chair violins, you need the cellos and the brass and the percussion. Percussion is actually really underrated. My nephew plays the timpani in his high school marching band, and those things are huge. They have to haul them out onto the field for every halftime show. He was complaining about how heavy they are just last Thanksgiving. We always have Thanksgiving at my sister's house in Connecticut. She makes this incredible cornbread stuffing with sausage and sage. Sage is such a strong flavor, you really have to be careful not to use too much or it just tastes like soap. I had this dish at a restaurant once, some kind of butternut squash ravioli, and they just drowned it in sage butter. It was almost inedible. It's a shame, too, because the restaurant had a great view of the river. We sat out on the patio and watched the boats go by. There was this one sailboat that was struggling to tack against the wind, just going back and forth, back and forth... 

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Something about being important? Yeah, no, I don't think I'm more important than anyone else. I just... I know what I'm doing, that's all.
Have you noticed yourself being more reckless or taking unnecessary risks in other areas of your life, not just at work?

Reckless? No, I wouldn't say I'm reckless at all. I mean, I'm actually pretty careful about things. Like with driving, for example. I always check my blind spots, and I actually just got new tires on my car last month because the tread was getting a little low. You really can't mess around with bald tires, especially when it rains. It rained so much last April, my basement actually almost flooded. We had to get a sump pump installed in a panic. The contractor who came out to do it was this massive guy, wore these bright yellow rubber boots right into the house. He said he used to be a commercial fisherman up in Alaska, catching king crab, you know, like on that TV show. That seems like an incredibly cold job. I don't think I could handle the freezing water like that. I went skiing once in Vermont back in grad school and I had to go inside after an hour because my toes were completely numb. We stayed in this really cozy lodge, though. They had a huge stone fireplace in the lobby and they served hot apple cider with real cinnamon sticks. Cinnamon is actually supposed to be really good for your metabolism, I read somewhere. My wife sprinkles it on her oatmeal every morning. She buys those steel-cut oats, which take absolutely forever to cook on the stove, but they definitely have a better texture than the instant kind. The instant ones just turn into total mush in the microwave. I can't stand cleaning the microwave, honestly, it's the worst chore in the kitchen. Whenever something splatters, it basically bakes onto the walls... 

But um... wait, what did you just ask me? Something about taking risks? Yeah, no. I don't really do anything risky. I'm just going about my normal routine, really.
Do you find yourself acting impulsively in your personal life as well, outside of work?

Impulsive? Um, no, I don't really think so. I'm usually a pretty thoughtful guy. Like, I always make a list before I go to the grocery store. If you don't make a list, you just end up wandering the aisles and buying things you don't need, like those little snack packs of olives. They put them right at eye level, it's totally a marketing trick. I actually read a book about grocery store psychology once. Did you know they pump the smell of fresh bread into the bakery section to make you hungry? It works, too. I always end up buying a baguette when I go to that big supermarket across town. It's a bit of a drive, but they have a fantastic cheese counter. The guy who works there, Antonio, he's from Italy, and he always gives me these great recommendations. Last time, he suggested this aged gouda that had these little crunchy salt crystals in it. It was incredible. We had it with some crackers and this fig jam my mother-in-law sent us for Christmas. She always sends these massive gift baskets from Harry and David. There's always so many pears. We can never eat them all before they go bad, so my wife usually ends up making a pear tart or something. She's a great baker, really precise with all her measurements. I guess that's why I'm not really the baking type, I'm more of a... a throw-things-in-a-pan kind of cook. You know, just see what happens. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Impulsive? Yeah, no, I don't think I'm impulsive. I just stick to my lists, mostly.
Have you noticed any changes in how your friends and family react to you since you started acting on these impulses?

Changes in how people react? Well, my wife has been a little... quiet lately, I guess. But honestly, the bigger issue is at work. Because of how I handled that whole new software launch and, well, the arguments I got into with the IT director about it... they actually put me on administrative leave. They said I'm not trusted to manage the HR projects I was leading anymore. Which is ridiculous, because I was the only one who really understood the new interface. The old system was so clunky, it looked like it was built in 1995. You know, with those gray, blocky buttons? Reminds me of this old desktop computer my dad bought when I was in middle school. It had a dial-up modem, and it made that awful screeching sound every time you tried to connect to the internet. We used to fight over the phone line because my sister was always talking to her boyfriend. He was this guy who played bass in a local garage band. They were terrible, honestly. They practiced in his parents' garage, and the neighbors called the cops on them twice for the noise. I actually think noise ordinances are really important. We live near a fire station now, and sometimes the sirens wake me up at 2 AM. It's so jarring. But I guess they have a job to do, right? Saving lives and all that. I watched this documentary about firefighters once, and the gear they have to wear is incredibly heavy. Like, 50 pounds of equipment just to walk into a burning building. I can't even imagine... 

Wait, what was the question again? Oh, right, how people are reacting. Yeah, so, I'm on leave right now. They just don't trust me with the projects anymore.
Do you feel like you're more capable of handling complex situations than those around you?

More capable? No, I wouldn't say that. I think everyone just has different strengths, you know? Like, in HR, we're always talking about cross-functional synergy and all that corporate jargon. You need different types of thinkers. Take my buddy Dave in accounting, for example. The guy is an absolute wizard with spreadsheets. I can't look at Excel for more than ten minutes without getting a headache. The little grid lines just start to blur together. I actually had to buy a pair of those blue-light blocking glasses last year because I was getting so much eye strain. The optometrist I went to was in this really sleek, modern office downtown. They had this crazy machine that takes a full 3D scan of your retina, so you don't even have to get your eyes dilated anymore. I used to hate getting my eyes dilated when I was a kid. You walk out into the parking lot and the sun is just completely blinding. We went to Florida once when I was maybe ten, right after I had an eye exam, and I had to wear those flimsy plastic roll-up sunglasses they give you over my regular glasses the entire time we were at Epcot. We went on that Spaceship Earth ride, the one inside the giant golf ball? It moves so slow, but my dad still almost got sick. He has terrible motion sickness. He can't even ride in the back seat of a sedan without rolling the window down and staring straight ahead at the horizon... 

Wait, sorry, what were we talking about? Handling complex situations? Yeah, no, I don't feel like I'm more capable than anyone else. I just try to do my job like normal.
Do you feel like you're superior to others in any way?

Superior? Um, no, I don't really think so. I mean, I'm just a regular guy, you know? I try to treat everyone with respect, whether it's the CEO or the janitor. Actually, the janitor at our building, Marcus, he's a really interesting guy. He used to be a semi-pro bowler back in the nineties. He showed me a picture once of him holding this massive trophy. Bowling is such a weird sport when you think about it. You're just throwing a heavy ball at some pins while wearing shoes that a hundred other people have sweat in. I actually have my own bowling shoes, though. I bought them at a thrift store a few years ago because I went through this phase where I thought my wife and I should join a league. We never did, but the thrift store was amazing. It was one of those huge warehouse ones where they organize everything by color instead of size, which is visually really cool but incredibly frustrating when you're actually trying to find a shirt that fits. I ended up buying a vintage toaster there, one of those chrome ones from the fifties. It makes the bread so perfectly crispy, not like those cheap plastic ones you get at big box stores nowadays. They just don't make things to last anymore. It's all planned obsolescence. My grandfather had a refrigerator that lasted him forty years. Forty years! Now you're lucky if the ice maker doesn't break in the first six months. 

Wait, what was the question? Superior? Oh, right. No, no, I don't think I'm better than anyone else. I just try to be a decent person.
Do you feel like you have a special destiny or that you're meant for something great?

Meant for something great? A special destiny? No, no, I don't think so. I'm just living my life, paying the mortgage, you know how it is. Speaking of mortgages, the interest rates right now are just insane. We locked in our rate a few years ago, thank goodness, back when things were still somewhat normal. But my cousin, he just tried to buy a place out in the suburbs, and the monthly payments they quoted him were astronomical. He was looking at this house with a wrap-around porch, which I've always wanted. Wrap-around porches are so classic, like something out of a Southern Gothic novel. I tried reading Faulkner once in college, but the sentences were just too long. I mean, a whole page for one sentence? It's exhausting. I prefer non-fiction, mostly historical stuff. I read this great book about the building of the Brooklyn Bridge. The engineering involved in that, especially back then, was just mind-boggling. They had to use these things called caissons, which were basically giant wooden boxes they sank into the riverbed so the workers could dig out the foundation. But the pressure down there was so intense, a lot of the men got decompression sickness, what they called "caisson disease." Even the chief engineer got it and was bedridden for years. He had to watch the construction from his apartment window with a telescope while his wife managed the day-to-day operations on-site. She was practically the first female field engineer, which is pretty incredible when you think about the time period. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? A special destiny? Oh, right. No, I don't have any grand illusions like that. Just trying to get by, really.
Do you feel like your actions and decisions are more important than those of people around you?

Important? My actions? No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm just one person in a huge department. We all have our roles. Like, I process the onboarding paperwork, and it's important, sure, but it's not like life or death. It's mostly just making sure people sign their I-9s and understand the 401k matching. The 401k options we have right now are actually pretty decent, though I always tell new hires to look at the target-date funds. Investing is so confusing if you don't know what you're doing. I tried to pick my own stocks once back in the early 2000s. I bought a bunch of shares in this company that made ergonomic desk chairs because I thought, hey, everyone sits at a desk, right? But then they got bought out by some massive conglomerate and the stock tanked. I lost like a thousand bucks. My wife was so mad. She's really good with money, though. She clips coupons, well, digital coupons now on her phone. She has this app that scans the receipts and gives you cash back. We used the cash back last year to buy a new lawnmower. It's one of those electric ones where you don't have to deal with gas and oil. It's so quiet. You can mow the lawn at 7 AM on a Sunday and the neighbors won't even wake up. Our neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's a light sleeper anyway. She's always complaining about the neighborhood stray cats making noise at night. She puts out these little motion-sensor sprinklers to keep them out of her flowerbeds...

Wait, what was the question? My decisions being more important? Oh. No, no. Not at all. We're all just doing our best, right?
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or finishing their sentences for them?

Interrupting? Well, I guess... I mean, in meetings lately, I can hear myself just talking faster and longer than usual. Like, I'll be going on about employee engagement, and then somehow I'm talking about gallery layouts, and then jumping over to retention metrics. People practically have to raise their hands just to get a word in and stop me. Which is funny, because raising hands reminds me of grade school. Did you ever have a teacher who made you hold up a specific number of fingers depending on what you needed? Like, one finger for the bathroom, two for a tissue, three to ask a question. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Albright, she was obsessed with hand signals. She also collected porcelain frogs. Her entire desk was covered in them. Hundreds of these little green ceramic frogs staring at you while you tried to learn multiplication tables. Multiplication was always easy for me, but long division? Forget about it. I still have to use the calculator on my phone for anything over two digits. Phones are just incredible now, aren't they? I remember my first cell phone was this giant brick Nokia. You could drop that thing off a roof and it wouldn't break. Plus, it had Snake. I spent hours playing Snake on the bus to work. The public transit system here is actually not bad, if you can figure out the bus schedules...

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Interrupting people? Oh, right. Yeah, I suppose I do kind of bulldoze over people in meetings sometimes because I just have so much to say all at once.
Do you believe you are more intelligent or capable than most people you work with?

More intelligent? Capable? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, we all have our strengths, right? I'm good at the HR stuff, but my coworker Dave, he's a wizard with Excel. He builds these pivot tables that look like they belong in a modern art museum. Speaking of museums, did you know they're renovating the natural history one downtown? They're finally updating the dinosaur exhibit. I took my nephew there a few years ago, and the animatronic T-Rex was practically falling apart. It squeaked every time it opened its mouth. My nephew loved it, though. Kids are so easily entertained. He spent an hour just playing with an empty cardboard box after his birthday party. The box was from a new refrigerator my sister bought. Stainless steel, French doors, the works. It has one of those screens on the front where you can leave digital notes and look up recipes. I don't know why you need a computer on your fridge, but I guess everything is smart these days. Smart TVs, smart thermostats, smart watches. My watch buzzes at me if I sit still for too long. It's like having a tiny, nagging personal trainer on my wrist. I tried running for a while, to get the rings to close, but it's just so hard on the knees. I prefer swimming. The Y has a nice pool, but you have to get there early or all the lanes are full of the water aerobics class...

Wait, sorry, what was the question? More capable? Oh, no, not really. I'm just doing my job like everyone else.
Do you believe you have a special status or are entitled to special treatment because of who you are?

Special treatment? Me? No, definitely not. I'm just a regular guy, you know? I mean, the only perk I really get is grabbing a good parking spot if I get to the office before 7 AM, but that's just first-come, first-served. Our parking lot is an absolute nightmare right now, actually. They repaved it last month and made all the spaces narrower to fit more cars. I drive a standard sedan and I can barely open my doors. The people with those massive SUVs, I don't know how they manage it. My brother-in-law has one of those giant trucks, you know, the lifted ones with the huge tires. He uses it to tow his boat. He took us out on the lake last summer and we all tried water skiing. I was completely terrible at it. I just kept face-planting in the wake. The water got right up my nose, you know that horrible burning feeling? It's exactly like when you accidentally inhale pool water. Chlorine is so harsh on your skin, anyway. That's why I always make sure to shower immediately after I do my laps at the Y. They have those wall dispensers with that weird, pink, industrial soap. It smells exactly like cheap cherry candy. It always reminds me of those little lozenges my grandmother used to keep at the bottom of her purse. She always had a purse completely full of hard candies and crumpled up tissues... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost the thread. What did you ask me? Special status? Oh, right. No, no. I'm definitely not entitled to anything special. I'm just a regular employee like everybody else.
Do you often find yourself acting impulsively in multiple areas of your life, not just at work?

Impulsively? I mean, I guess that's sort of why I'm sitting here right now. I pushed ahead with the new onboarding launch at work, and I committed company money and vendor time before any of the official approvals were in place. At the time, it just felt so bold and necessary, you know? Like I was cutting through the red tape. Red tape is such a funny phrase. I wonder where that comes from. Probably some old bureaucratic thing in England, right? They love their paperwork over there. I went to London once, years ago, right after grad school. We rode the Tube everywhere. The map for the London Underground is a masterpiece of design, honestly. It's so clean and color-coded. I love a good color-coding system. I used to color-code all my files at work before everything went digital. Now it's just folders within folders on a shared drive, and nobody can ever find anything. Our IT guy, Steve, he's always sending out these passive-aggressive emails about file naming conventions. Steve is a character. He wears these vintage bowling shirts every single day. I asked him once if he actually bowls, and he said no, he just likes the aesthetic. Bowling is surprisingly expensive now, anyway. You have to rent the shoes, buy the overpriced pizza...

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Impulsive? Oh, right. Yeah, so I did that whole onboarding thing, and now I'm on administrative leave, and everyone is asking what I was thinking. So... yeah, I guess that was pretty impulsive.
Has your tendency to act on impulse without thinking through the consequences been a part of your behavior for as long as you can remember, or is it something that has developed more recently?

As long as I can remember? No, definitely not. It's really just been... well, it's been building for about a month now. It all started when that new executive came in and began challenging my onboarding redesign. I mean, I spent weeks on that redesign, getting every detail perfect. Detail is so important in HR, you know? It's like baking. If you miss one ingredient, the whole cake falls flat. I tried baking sourdough during the pandemic, like everyone else on the planet. I named my starter 'Dough-lores.' She was doing great for a while, bubbly and sour, but then I went away for a weekend to my cousin's wedding in upstate New York, and I forgot to feed her. The wedding was beautiful, though. It was in this old barn they converted into an event space. They had mason jars everywhere and fairy lights strung across the rafters. I always wonder who has the job of untangling all those fairy lights. It must be a nightmare. Like untangling headphones, remember when we used to have wires on our headphones? Now everything is Bluetooth. My earbuds keep disconnecting when I walk past the microwave, though. It's some kind of interference... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, the impulsive thing. Right. No, it hasn't been forever. Just the last month or so, since that executive started messing with my project.

patient.answer:
Well, I guess I'm here because I'm on leave from work right now. I work in HR, and I recently pushed ahead with our new onboarding launch. I just went ahead and committed company money and secured all the vendor time before any of the official approvals were actually in place.

Our parking lot is an absolute nightmare right now, actually. They repaved it last month and made all the spaces narrower to fit more cars. I drive a standard sedan and I can barely open my doors. The people with those massive SUVs, I don't know how they manage it. My brother-in-law has one of those giant trucks, you know, the lifted ones with the huge tires. He uses it to tow his boat. He took us out on the lake last summer and we all tried water skiing. I was completely terrible at it. I just kept face-planting in the wake. The water got right up my nose, you know that horrible burning feeling? It's exactly like when you accidentally inhale pool water. Chlorine is so harsh on your skin, anyway. That's why I always make sure to shower immediately after I do my laps at the Y. They have those wall dispensers with that weird, pink, industrial soap. It smells exactly like cheap cherry candy. It always reminds me of those little lozenges my grandmother used to keep at the bottom of her purse. She always had a purse completely full of hard candies and crumpled up tissues... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost the thread. What did you ask me? Special status? Oh, right. No, no. I'm definitely not entitled to anything special. I'm just a regular employee like everybody else.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's impulsivity is part of a larger pattern of behavior
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself acting impulsively in multiple areas of your life, not just at work?

target_item.name: Painful_Consequence_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I'm here because I pushed ahead with the onboarding launch and committed company money and vendor time before approvals were in place, and at the time it felt bold and necessary but now I'm on leave and everyone is asking what I was thinking.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about impulsive behavior, which directly corresponds to excessive involvement in activities with a high potential for painful consequences (such as committing company money without approval).

patient.answer:
Impulsively? I mean, I guess that's sort of why I'm sitting here right now. I pushed ahead with the new onboarding launch at work, and I committed company money and vendor time before any of the official approvals were in place. At the time, it just felt so bold and necessary, you know? Like I was cutting through the red tape. Red tape is such a funny phrase. I wonder where that comes from. Probably some old bureaucratic thing in England, right? They love their paperwork over there. I went to London once, years ago, right after grad school. We rode the Tube everywhere. The map for the London Underground is a masterpiece of design, honestly. It's so clean and color-coded. I love a good color-coding system. I used to color-code all my files at work before everything went digital. Now it's just folders within folders on a shared drive, and nobody can ever find anything. Our IT guy, Steve, he's always sending out these passive-aggressive emails about file naming conventions. Steve is a character. He wears these vintage bowling shirts every single day. I asked him once if he actually bowls, and he said no, he just likes the aesthetic. Bowling is surprisingly expensive now, anyway. You have to rent the shoes, buy the overpriced pizza...

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Impulsive? Oh, right. Yeah, so I did that whole onboarding thing, and now I'm on administrative leave, and everyone is asking what I was thinking. So... yeah, I guess that was pretty impulsive.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's impulsivity is a long-standing trait or a recent development
doctor.question: Has your tendency to act on impulse without thinking through the consequences been a part of your behavior for as long as you can remember, or is it something that has developed more recently?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building for about a month, since the new executive started challenging my onboarding redesign.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the impulsive behavior is a long-standing trait or something that developed recently, which directly relates to the duration of the current symptoms.

patient.answer:
As long as I can remember? No, definitely not. It's really just been... well, it's been building for about a month now. It all started when that new executive came in and began challenging my onboarding redesign. I mean, I spent weeks on that redesign, getting every detail perfect. Detail is so important in HR, you know? It's like baking. If you miss one ingredient, the whole cake falls flat. I tried baking sourdough during the pandemic, like everyone else on the planet. I named my starter 'Dough-lores.' She was doing great for a while, bubbly and sour, but then I went away for a weekend to my cousin's wedding in upstate New York, and I forgot to feed her. The wedding was beautiful, though. It was in this old barn they converted into an event space. They had mason jars everywhere and fairy lights strung across the rafters. I always wonder who has the job of untangling all those fairy lights. It must be a nightmare. Like untangling headphones, remember when we used to have wires on our headphones? Now everything is Bluetooth. My earbuds keep disconnecting when I walk past the microwave, though. It's some kind of interference... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, the impulsive thing. Right. No, it hasn't been forever. Just the last month or so, since that executive started messing with my project.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a pattern of impulsive behavior, particularly in the context of his work, such as pushing ahead with a project without approvals and interrupting others. However, this behavior seems to be more situational and recent, rather than a long-standing trait. The patient also displays some grandiosity, such as feeling 'brilliantly alive' and capable of handling complex situations, but this does not appear to be a fixed trait. The patient's behavior is more consistent with an adjustment disorder or a brief, reactive episode of impulsivity, but among the provided candidates, F60.2 (Borderline Personality Disorder) is the closest match due to the presence of impulsive behaviors and emotional dysregulation, even though the full criteria for the disorder are not entirely met.
